title: Structuring a modern AI team — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs
talk_summary: A team-structure and hiring talk from a Wisedocs ML lead arguing that domain-aware generalists beat elite researchers for most companies, and that teams should be built around identified bottlenecks rather than trends. It contains almost no engineering mechanism, but a few transferable ideas about context ownership, verification, and feedback-loop shortening apply loosely to agent design.

takeaways.what_they_do: Splits roles into those that hold context (domain knowledge, accountability) and those that act on it (execution), and argues you need enough of the former to verify the latter's output.
takeaways.evidence_quote: One is to hold context and the other is to act on context.

takeaways.what_they_do: Argues that even with huge context windows, you need expertise grounded in context to verify that agent output is correct, so verification cannot be fully delegated to a generic model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need expertise to be able to verify that this context and this execution is correct

takeaways.technique: Identify the bottleneck before adding capacity
takeaways.what_they_do: Frames team building as first naming the actual bottleneck (shipping, retention, scalability, reliability) and staffing to it, rather than copying trends.
takeaways.evidence_quote: identify to yourself what is your bottleneck? What is stopping you from achieving success?

takeaways.what_they_do: Replaces static product requirement docs with quick functional prototypes that surface edge cases early, shortening the PM-engineer feedback loop.
takeaways.evidence_quote: go from static product requirements to functional prototypes that take those details and elicit them

takeaways.technique: Domain experts write the use cases/evals
takeaways.what_they_do: Moves domain experts from giving feedback to authoring the use cases and evaluations themselves, with enough literacy to work with models directly.
takeaways.evidence_quote: domain experts aren't just providing input and feedback that they're the ones writing the use cases defining them
